Enhanced SS-factor for the 14N(p,γ)15(p,\gamma)^{15}O reaction and its impact on the solar composition problem

Abstract

The solar composition problem has puzzled astrophysicists for more than 20 years. Recent measurements of carbon-nitrogen-oxygen (CNO) neutrinos by the Borexino experiment show a ∼2​σ\sim 2\sigma tension with the “low-metallicity” determinations. 14N(p,γ)15(p,\gamma)^{15}O, the slowest reaction in the CNO cycle, plays a crucial role in the standard solar model (SSM) calculations of CNO neutrino fluxes. Here we report a direct measurement of the 14N(p,γ)15(p,\gamma)^{15}O reaction, in which SS-factors for all transitions were simultaneously determined in the energy range of Ep=110−260E_{p}=110-260 keV for the first time. Our results resolve previous discrepancies in the ground-state transition, yielding a zero-energy SS-factor S114​(0)=1.92±0.08S_{114}(0)=1.92\pm 0.08 keV b which is 14% higher than the 1.68±0.141.68\pm 0.14 keV b recommended in Solar Fusion III (SF-III). With our S114S_{114} values, the SSM B23-GS98, and the latest global analysis of solar neutrino measurements, the C and N photospheric abundance determined by the Borexino experiment is updated to NCN=(4.45−0.61+0.69)×10−4N_{\mathrm{CN}}=({4.45}^{+0.69}_{-0.61})\times 10^{-4}. This new NCNN_{\mathrm{CN}} value agrees well with latest “high-metallicity” composition, however, is also consistent with the “low-metallicity” determination within ∼1​σ\sim 1\sigma C.L., indicating that the solar metallicity problem remains an open question. In addition, the significant reduction in the uncertainty of S114S_{114} paves the way for the precise determination of the CN abundance in future large-volume solar neutrino measurements.

The study of solar properties not only provides a benchmark for exploring the vast stellar domains of the cosmos, but also advances a broad range of related disciplines. Solar metallicity, defined as the ratio of elements heavier than helium to hydrogen in the Sun, serves as a key parameter in the standard solar models (SSMs), directly influencing our understanding of solar properties. Early solar metallicities determined by modeling the spectra observed from the solar photosphere agreed with estimates from helioseimology measurements. However, the metallicities reported by the works [1, 2, 3] using the advanced techniques consistently exhibit a 30% to 40% reduction compared to the value given by traditional modeling [4]. This discrepancy, known as the “solar composition problem” or “solar abundance problem”, has puzzled astrophysicists for over two decades, prompting ongoing investigations from multiple perspectives. In this letter, we follow the statements in Solar Fusion III (SF-III) [11] and adopt the metallicities from Asplund et al. [3] and Magg et al. [6] to represent the low-metallicity (LZ) and high-metallicity (HZ) compositions, respectively.

Solar neutrino measurements provide direct insights into the solar interior, opening a new approach to resolving the solar composition problem. Among the various types of solar neutrinos, carbon-nitrogen-oxygen (CNO) neutrinos are considered the most effective tool for studying solar metallicity [7, 8]. Remarkable progress has been achieved by recent Borexino experiments [9, 10]. The measured CNO neutrino flux, combined with the predictions of SSMs, has been used to derive the CN abundance with respect to the H abundance NCNN_{\rm{CN}} in the photosphere of the sun. The result, NCN=(5.81−0.94+1.22×10−4)N_{\rm{CN}}=(5.81^{+1.22}_{-0.94}\times 10^{-4}) [11], shows a preference for HZ compositions and a ∼2​σ\sim 2\sigma tension with the LZ determinations.

14N(p,γ)15(p,\gamma)^{15}O, the slowest reaction in the CNO cycle, directly controls the production rate of CNO neutrinos [12]. Consequently, the SS-factor of this reaction, S114S_{114}, plays a crucial role in the SSMs calculation and the estimation of the NCNN_{\rm{CN}}. Furthermore, due to the crucial influence on the timescale of hydrogen burning in stars more massive than the Sun [13], precise S114S_{114} values can help us better understand the age and evolution of star clusters and galaxies [14, 15]. After extensive efforts over the past decades, S114S_{114} values have been significantly improved. The latest compilation SF-III [11] recommended a zero energy SS-factor of S114​(0)=1.68±0.14S_{114}(0)=1.68\pm 0.14 keV b. Although it represents a secondary contribution to the uncertainty in estimating NCNN_{\rm{CN}}, this 8.4% error will become a bottleneck as CN neutrino data are improved by future large-volume experiments [11].

Currently, the improvement in the precision of S114S_{114} is limited by the incomplete understanding of the ground-state transition at low energies, which are strongly influenced by a sub-threshold resonance at Ex=6.79E_{x}=6.79 MeV. In 1987, Schröder et al. [16] obtained a large zero-energy SS-factor for the ground-state transition S114g.s.​(0)=1.55±0.34S_{114}^{\rm{g.s.}}(0)=1.55\pm 0.34 keV b from direct measurement. However, this result was dramatically revised to 0.08−0.06+0.130.08^{+0.13}_{-0.06} keV b by Angulo and Descouvemont [15]. In 2005, two direct measurements were performed by Runkle et al. [5] and Imbriani et al. [6] at lower energies, respectively. The S114g.s.​(0)=0.49±0.08S_{114}^{\rm{g.s.}}(0)=0.49\pm 0.08 keV b obtained in Runkle et al. [5] is significantly higher than the S114g.s.​(0)=0.25±0.06S_{114}^{\rm{g.s.}}(0)=0.25\pm 0.06 keV b reported in Imbriani et al. [6]. The main discrepancy between these two measurements [5, 6] lies in the trend of the SS-factor around Ec.m.=200E_{\mathrm{c.m.}}=200 keV. Several measurements [13, 14, 22, 16] of excitation function and angular distributions at higher energies have provided additional constraints for RR-matrix fitting. Moreover, efforts have been made to measure the lifetime and width of the 6.79 MeV state in 15O [24, 25, 26, 27, 10, 29], but these efforts have not yet led to significant progress.

In this Letter, we report a direct measurement of the 14N(p,γ)15(p,\gamma)^{15}O cross sections at low energies. The SS-factors for all transitions were simultaneously determined through a multi-channel Bayesian analysis of the obtained γ\gamma spectra. Our results resolve the discrepancies in the ground-state transition and provide better constraints for RR-matrix fitting. The updated S114S_{114} values were then used to investigate the solar composition problem.

The experiment was conducted at Hefei 350 kV accelerator facility [1] with a ∼2\sim 2 mA proton beam and TiN targets. The γ\gamma spectra were measured at Ep=110−260E_{p}=110-260 keV using the second configuration of the Large Modular BGO Detector Array (LAMBDA-II) with a summing method [31, 32, 33]. The experimental setup and detailed procedures are provided in the Supplemental Material.

In the data analysis, improvements were made to the previously used summing method [31, 32, 33]. By taking advantage of the high granularity of LAMBDA-II (16 modules), the γ−γ\gamma-\gamma coincidences and number of triggered modules (nhit) were used to distinguish the events from different transitions in 14N(p,γ)15(p,\gamma)^{15}O. These constraints helped further reduce the interference from laboratory background, beam-induced background and other transitions. Figure 1 shows the γ−γ\gamma-\gamma coincidence spectra obtained at Ep=180E_{p}=180 keV. Four transitions following double cascades, including RC→\rightarrow6.79→\rightarrow0, RC→\rightarrow6.17→\rightarrow0, RC→\rightarrow5.24→\rightarrow0 and RC→\rightarrow5.18→\rightarrow0 can be clearly identified in Fig. 1(a) gated by nhit=2. Two transitions following triple cascades, RC→\rightarrow7.28→\rightarrow5.24→\rightarrow0 and RC→\rightarrow6.86→\rightarrow5.24→\rightarrow0, are also identified in the γ−γ\gamma-\gamma coincidence spectrum gated by nhit=3, with an additional 5.24±0.255.24\pm 0.25 MeV gate on one of the triggered modules, as shown in Fig. 1(b).

Figure 2 shows the sum spectrum (the sum of the energies) and the single spectrum (superimposing the spectra from each module) spectra obtained at Ep=180E_{p}=180 keV. The single spectra were gated by different nhit values and corresponding γ−γ\gamma-\gamma coincidence gates.

We applied a Bayesian approach to perform a multichannel fit to the four γ\gamma spectra shown in Fig. 2, using the Bayesian Analysis Toolkit (BAT) [34]. The shapes of fractional contribution from each transition to the corresponding spectrum were simulated using the GEANT4 program [35, 36, 37]. Both the laboratory background and beam-induced background were included in the fitting, as shown in Fig. 2(a). The laboratory background was reduced to a negligible level (∼1×10−2\sim 1\times 10^{-2} keV-1h-1 around the sum peak of 14N(p,γ)15(p,\gamma)^{15}O) by several measures detailed in the Supplemental Material, except for the measurements at the lowest few energy points. The beam-induced background was obtained using corresponding targets at the same beam energy, with the exception of D(p,γ)3(p,\gamma)^{3}He, which was constructed via Monte Carlo simulation.

The fractional contributions from different transitions and background fitted using BAT are represented by different colored areas in Fig. 2. The single peaks corresponding to the 5.18, 5.24, 6.17, and 6.79 MeV transitions are clearly visible in Fig. 2(c), with minimal interference from other transitions. Although the contributions of the 5.18 and 5.24 transitions cannot be directly separated, they were effectively constrained by the shapes of the γ\gamma peaks around 2.3 and 5.2 MeV, as shown in the inset of Fig. 2(c). Fig. 2(d) presents the fitting of the 6.86 and 7.28 MeV transitions following triple cascades, where considerable disturbances from the 6.79 and 5.18 transitions are found. Fig. 2(b) illustrates the fitting of the single peak corresponding to the ground-state transition, with approximately half of the contribution arises from the sum-in effect of other transitions. To validate the accuracy of the sum-in effect estimation, the branching ratios for the Ep=278E_{p}=278 keV resonance were analyzed with the same process. As listed in the Supplemental Material, the obtained branching ratios are in agreement with those reported in previous works [5, 6, 13, 8], including the ground-state transition.

Using the reaction counts extracted from BAT fitting, the SS-factors for each transition are calculated. In the calculation, the number of 14N atoms and the beam energy loss (Δ​E\Delta E) in the target were derived from regular yield scans of the Ep=278E_{p}=278 keV resonance and the trend of the target degradation, as detailed in the Supplemental Material. The SS-factors obtained in this work were compared with data from previous studies [7, 5, 6] in Fig. 3. The error bars represent statistical uncertainties only, which arise from the BAT fitting, beam energy calibration, Δ​E\Delta E determination, the non-uniformity in the target distribution, and the target degradation trends. Our total SS-factors are consistent with the values reported by Bemmerer et al. [7], although they are systematically slightly lower. For individual transitions, the SS-factors for the 6.17 and 6.79 MeV transitions agree with those from Runkle et al. [5] and Imbriani et al. [6]. The SS-factors for the 5.18 MeV transition are consistent with Imbriani et al. [6] except for a few low-energy points. Data for the 5.24, 6.86, and 7.28 MeV transitions are reported in this energy range for the first time. For the ground-state transition, our results are systematically higher than those of Imbriani et al. [6] at Ec.m.<210E_{\rm{c.m.}}<210 keV but agree with the data from Runkle et al. [5] at Ec.m.=180−240E_{\rm{c.m.}}=180-240 keV.

The extrapolation of SS-factors for each transition to zero energy was performed using an RR-Matrix analysis with the code AZURE2 [40]. To impose basic constraints on the RR-matrix fit, in addition to our experimental data, we included data from Runkle et al. [5], Li et al. [14], and Schröder et al. [16] into the fit, thereby constraining the shapes and strengths in the higher energy regions. Due to the inconsistency at low energies, we excluded the data points from Imbriani et al. [6] from the fit. Given that our focus is on the fitting results below the 278 keV resonance, we allowed 28 parameters that significantly affect the SS-factors in the low-energy region to vary during the fit, based on the full set of parameters from Li et al. [14] as the initial values. The specific parameters used in the fitting procedure are provided in the Supplemental Material. As shown in Fig. 3, the RR-matrix fits successfully reproduce both the high-energy data and the low-energy data provided by this study, with a reduced χ2\chi^{2} of 3.85 for all data points and 1.42 for the data points from this study.

The zero-energy total SS-factor was determined to be 1.92±0.081.92\pm 0.08 keV b, where the uncertainty includes 2.2% statistical uncertainty and 3.4% systematic uncertainty. This value is consistent with data reported by Angulo and Descouvemont [15], however, higher than those from other experiments [6, 5, 13, 16], as shown in Fig. 4. This increase is primarily attributed to the enhancement of the ground-state transition at low energies and the inclusion of more weak transitions such as 6.86 and 7.28 MeV. Specifically, our new S114​(0)S_{114}(0) is 14% higher than the value recommended in SF-III [11]. Moreover, the improved constraints provided by the comprehensive measurement of all transitions in the RR-Matrix fitting have significantly reduced the uncertainties in the extrapolation of the SS-factors. The zero-energy SS-factors for individual transitions are listed in the Supplemental Material.

To investigate the impact of the new S114S_{114} values on the solar composition problem, the C and N abundances relative to H (NCNN_{\rm{CN}}) in the photosphere of the sun were calculated following the method from previous work [10]:

NCNNCNSSM\displaystyle\frac{N_{\rm{CN}}}{N_{\rm{CN}}^{\rm{SSM}}} =(ΦO/ΦOSSM)(ΦB/ΦBSSM)0.769×{1±[0.065(nucl)\displaystyle=\frac{\left(\Phi_{\rm{O}}/\Phi_{\rm{O}}^{\rm{SSM}}\right)}{\left(\Phi_{\rm{B}}/\Phi_{\rm{B}}^{\rm{SSM}}\right)^{0.769}}\times\left\{1\pm\left[0.065\,(\mathrm{nucl})\right.\right. (1)
⊕0.005(env)⊕0.027(diff)]}\displaystyle\oplus\left.\left.0.005\,(\mathrm{env})\oplus 0.027\,(\mathrm{diff})\right]\right\}

where NCNSSMN_{\rm{CN}}^{\rm{SSM}} is the NCNN_{\rm{CN}} value adopted in the SSM calculation. ΦO\Phi_{\rm{O}} and ΦB\Phi_{\rm{B}} represent the measured fluxes of 15O and 8B neutrinos, respectively. ΦOSSM\Phi_{\rm{O}}^{\rm{SSM}} and ΦBSSM\Phi_{\rm{B}}^{\rm{SSM}} denote the corresponding values predicted by the SSM. The terms in curly brackets quantify the uncertainties due to nuclear, environmental, and diffusion effects, summed in quadrature. Compared to Appel et al. [10], the nuclear terms have been updated based on our new S114S_{114} values and the latest SS-factor recommendations from SF-III [11].

The predicted changes in solar neutrino flux due to variations in S114S_{114} follow a well-determined power-law relationship [41, 42],

ΦBnew,SSM=ΦBSSM×xS1140.007ΦOnew,SSM=ΦOSSM×xS1141.051\begin{array}[]{l}\Phi_{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{new},\mathrm{SSM}}=\Phi_{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{SSM}}\times x_{S_{114}}^{0.007}\\ \Phi_{\mathrm{O}}^{\mathrm{new},\mathrm{SSM}}=\Phi_{\mathrm{O}}^{\mathrm{SSM}}\times x_{S_{114}}^{1.051}\end{array} (2)

where xS114x_{S_{114}} represents the ratio of the updated SS-factor to the previously adopted SS-factor in the SSM calculation. Therefore, the impact of our new S114S_{114} values on the ΦBSSM\Phi_{\rm{B}}^{\rm{SSM}} and ΦOSSM\Phi_{\rm{O}}^{\rm{SSM}} can be estimated without performing additional SSM calculation. Based on the B23-GS98 predictions [42], with the new S114S_{114} values, these fluxes are updated to ΦBnew,SSM=5.029×106​cm−2​s−1\Phi_{\rm{B}}^{\rm{new,SSM}}=5.029\times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{cm}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1} and ΦOnew,SSM=2.296×108​cm−2​s−1\Phi_{\rm{O}}^{\rm{new,SSM}}=2.296\times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{cm}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}, respectively.

Combining these updated ΦBnew,SSM\Phi_{\rm{B}}^{\rm{new,SSM}} and ΦOnew,SSM\Phi_{\rm{O}}^{\rm{new,SSM}}, the ΦB=5.20−0.10+0.10×106​cm−2​s−1\Phi_{\rm{B}}=5.20_{-0.10}^{+0.10}\times 10^{6}~\rm{cm}^{-2}\rm{s}^{-1} and ΦO=2.53−0.29+0.34×108​cm−2​s−1\Phi_{\rm{O}}=2.53_{-0.29}^{+0.34}\times 10^{8}~\rm{cm}^{-2}\rm{s}^{-1} from the recent global analysis of neutrino measurements [43], and the NCNSSM=4.143×10−4N_{\rm{CN}}^{\rm{SSM}}=4.143\times 10^{-4} provided by the GS98 [4], we derived a new C and N abundance of NCN=(4.45−0.61+0.69)×10−4N_{\rm{CN}}=({4.45}^{+0.69}_{-0.61})\times 10^{-4} using Eq. 1. This result is 23.4% lower than the previous value NCN=(5.81−0.94+1.22)×10−4N_{\rm{CN}}=({5.81}^{+1.22}_{-0.94})\times 10^{-4} reported by Basilico et al. [11], which is primarily attributed to the larger S114S_{114} determined in this work and the lower ΦO\Phi_{\rm{O}} updated in Ref. [43]. Due to the improvement in the precision of the S114S_{114} values in this work, although it remains the second contribution, the uncertainty from the nuclear cross section (6.5%) is now significantly smaller than that from the measured CNO neutrino flux (−11.5%+13.4%{}^{+13.4\%}_{-11.5\%}).

Figure 5 shows a comparison of the NCNN_{\mathrm{CN}} values derived from solar CNO neutrino measurements and those from HZ [6] and LZ [3] compositions. Compared to the previous result of Basilico et al. [11], the updated NCNN_{\rm{CN}} shows better agreement with the HZ value. More importantly, this new NCNN_{\rm{CN}} value is also consistent with the LZ value within the 1σ\sigma C.L., challenging the previous disfavor of the LZ compositions [10, 11]. Therefore, our result demonstrates that the current solar neutrino measurements are insufficient to draw a solid conclusion on the solar composition problem. Given that the uncertainty primarily arises from the measured 15O neutrino flux, further measurements of solar CNO neutrinos with higher precision are desired to address this issue.

In summary, we conducted a new comprehensive measurement of the 14N(p,γ)15(p,\gamma)^{15}O SS-factors at low energies. Using a multiple-channel Bayesian analysis, the SS-factors for all transitions in the energy range of Ep=110−260E_{p}=110-260 keV were simultaneously extracted for the first time. The data for the ground-state transition, with higher precision, resolved discrepancies found in previous works. RR-Matrix analysis of the new experimental results yields a higher and more precise S114S_{114}(0) value compared to that recommended in SF-III. The new S114S_{114} combined with the updated B23 SSM and latest globe determination of all solar neutrino fluxes significantly reduces the NCNN_{\rm{CN}} value determined by the CNO neutrino measurements. The updated NCNN_{\rm{CN}} value agrees well with that of the HZ composition but is also consistent with the LZ composition within 1​σ1\sigma C.L.. As a result, we conclude that the solar composition problem remains an open question, requiring more precise observational data on solar CNO neutrino for resolution. Furthermore, given the crucial role of the 14N(p,γ)15(p,\gamma)^{15}O reaction in the CNO cycle, the refined S114S_{114} values obtained in this work are expected to have significant impacts on several related astrophysical studies.

I. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP

The experiment was conducted at the 350 kV accelerator located at the Institute of Nuclear Energy Safety Technology (INEST) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences [1]. This accelerator can provide a proton beam with a maximum current of 5 mA within an energy range of 50-300  keV. During the low-energy measurements, the typical beam current on the target was 2 mA. The high voltage of the accelerator was calibrated using the Ep=278E_{p}=278 keV resonance of 14N(p,γ)15(p,\gamma)^{15}O and the Ep=151E_{p}=151 keV resonance of 18O(p,γ)19(p,\gamma)^{19}F. Figure 1 shows the experimental setup. The H1+ beam was collimated by two apertures (Φ\Phi15 mm and Φ\Phi10 mm) and directed towards TiN target with a diameter of 47.5 mm. Two Pb rings with thicknesses of 10 cm and 8 cm were installed behind the apertures to shield the γ\gamma rays produced by the beam bombarding the apertures. The target was directly cooled using flowing deionized water to control the temperature. A liquid nitrogen-cooled cold trap was extended near the target surface to minimize the carbon deposition on the target. A ring electrode with a negative voltage of 300 V was installed at the end of the cold trap to reduce the influence of the secondary electrons on the integral beam charge.

The second configuration of the large modular BGO detector array (LAMBDA-II) [2] was used to measure the γ\gamma rays emitted from the 14N(p,γ)15(p,\gamma)^{15}O reaction. LAMBDA-II consists of 48 identical modules, each containing a 6 cm×\times6 cm×\times12 cm BGO crystal, as shown in Fig. 1 The inner 16 modules served as the primary detector array, providing nearly complete coverage of the target. The outer 32 modules acted as an anti-coincidence detector array, effectively suppressing laboratory background. We employed the summing method in measurements, where the energies of the inner 16 modules were summed to obtain the sum spectrum, and the individual spectra from each module were superimposed to form the single spectrum. Calibration using a 137Cs source resulted in an energy resolution of 10.2% and a full energy peak efficiency of 53±153\pm 1% for the 662 keV sum peak. To reduce the laboratory background, a series of shielding and anti-coincidence measures were implemented:

1). All modules were embedded within a honeycomb-shaped block made of boron polyethylene, which effectively absorbed laboratory and cosmic ray-induced neutrons.

2). A 10 cm thick Pb shield provided full coverage to absorb the γ\gamma ray from the outside.

3). The five sides of the Pb shield, excluding the bottom, were covered with 5 cm thick plastic scintillators. An anti-window of 10 μ\mus following each trigger of plastic scintillators was used to veto muons and neutrons produced by muons.

By employing the above methods, the laboratory background was reduced by about 2 orders of magnitude at Eγ>5E_{\rm{\gamma}}>5 MeV, specifically to 1×10−21\times 10^{-2} keV-1h-1 around the sum peak of the 14N(p,γ)15(p,\gamma)^{15}O reaction. This significant reduction in background, along with the high-intensity proton beam, enabled the extension of the 14N(p,γ)15(p,\gamma)^{15}O measurement to low energies. For instance, the measured counts at the sum peak for 14N(p,γ)15(p,\gamma)^{15}O at Ep=125E_{p}=125 keV were 15 times higher than the laboratory background after applying the anti-coincidence method, as shown in Fig. 2.

The beam-induced background primarily originates from the beam bombarding the impurities in the target, including γ\gamma rays emitted by (p,γ)(p,\gamma) reactions on D, 11B, 12C, 13C, 15N, and 18O, as well as the (p,α​γ)(p,\alpha\gamma) reactions on 15N and 19F. Consequently, targets of Ti15N, Al182{}_{2}^{18}O3, natural C, F and B were prepared via different techniques to measure the corresponding beam-induced background. The γ\gamma rays produced by the beam bombarding the apertures are negligible due to significant attenuation by 8 cm Pb rings positioned behind them.

II. TARGET PROPERTIES

To minimize impurities in the target, various techniques were employed to fabricate solid nitrogen targets, including ion sputtering, low-pressure chemical vapor deposition (LPCVD), and filtered cathodic vacuum arc (FCVA). Among these, the TiN target prepared via FCVA exhibited the lowest impurity levels and the highest radiation resistance, making it the preferred method in this study. During the preparation, a thick Ti layer (>1​μ>1~\mum) was deposited on a 1 mm thick Ta substrate to prevent the proton beam from reaching the surface Ta2O5 layer. Subsequently, nitrogen gas was introduced into the vacuum chamber to combine with Ti ions and deposit a TiN foil on the Ti layer. The thickness of the TiN layer was adjusted by controlling the deposition time to achieve a ∼12\sim 12 keV energy loss at EpE_{p}=280 keV. Details of target preparation will be discussed in the forthcoming work [3]. As shown in Fig. 3, throughout the experiment, repeated scans of the Ep=278E_{p}=278 keV resonance yield curve for the 14N(p,γ)15(p,\gamma)^{15}O reaction were conducted after accumulating a certain amount of charge on the target. This was done to monitor target degradation, nitrogen content in the TiN target, and the energy loss of the proton beam.

The number of nitrogen nuclei in the target was calculated using the following formula:

AY=ns​λr22​ω​γA_{Y}=n_{s}\frac{\lambda_{r}^{2}}{2}\omega\gamma

where nsn_{s} represents the number of active target nuclei per cm², AYA_{Y} denotes the area under the resonance yield curve, λr\lambda_{r} is the de Broglie wavelength corresponding to the resonance energy, and ω​γ\omega\gamma represents the resonance strength. In determining nsn_{s}, a resonance strength of ω​γ278=13.0±0.4\omega\gamma_{278}=13.0\pm 0.4 meV was adopted. This value represents the weighted average of ω​γ278=13.2±0.6\omega\gamma_{278}=13.2\pm 0.6 meV obtained in the present study and the values reported in previous research [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10], as shown in Table 1. The averaging method was based on the approach used by SF III [11]. The systematic uncertainty of 2.9% associated with the nitrogen stopping power [12] was excluded from the weighted mean calculation and instead combined in quadrature with the weighted mean uncertainty to obtain the final uncertainty.

III. BRANCHING RATIOS OF THE Ep=278E_{p}=278 KEV RESONANCE

To accurately determine the branching ratios of resonance transitions, the angular correlation effects of γ\gamma-ray cascades between energy levels cannot be ignored. In our analysis, when using Geant4 simulations to determine the spectra of each transition component, we accounted for the theoretical angular correlation effects in the 6.17 MeV and 6.79 MeV transitions. Specifically, the angular correlation functions W6.17​(θ)=1+0.138​P2​(cos⁡θ)W_{6.17}(\theta)=1+0.138P_{2}(\cos\theta) and W6.79​(θ)=1+0.250​P2​(cos⁡θ)W_{6.79}(\theta)=1+0.250P_{2}(\cos\theta) were applied. By analyzing the results from multiple scans of the resonance for different targets, the branching ratios were finally determined, as shown in Table 2.
